background:
James: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes

Study notes · dates are approximate and scholars vary

At a glance

James is a practical letter about living faith, written by the leader of the Jerusalem church to Jewish believers scattered abroad. Its short, punchy sayings echo Jesus' Sermon on the Mount. It may be one of the earliest New Testament books, from the AD 40s, or from the late 50s.

QuestionTraditional viewNotes
AuthorJames, “a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:1)Traditionally James the brother of Jesus (Gal 1:19), who did not believe during Jesus' ministry (John 7:5) but saw the risen Lord (1 Cor 15:7).
DateAbout AD 45–49, or AD 55–62No mention of the Jerusalem council or Gentile controversies suggests an early date; others place it near James' death.
Written fromJerusalemJames led the Jerusalem church with the elders (Acts 15:13; 21:18).
Recipients“The twelve tribes which are of the Dispersion”Jewish Christians living outside Judea, many of them poor.
StyleWisdom literatureOver 50 commands in 108 verses; many images from farming, sea travel and everyday life.
James' deathAD 62Josephus says the high priest Ananus had James stoned in the gap between two Roman governors.

James insists that real faith shows itself in action: “faith, if it have not works, is dead in itself” (2:17).

Rich and poor in James' world

James speaks bluntly about wealth and poverty, which were sharp realities in first-century Judea and the diaspora.

  • Landowners and laborers. Much land was owned by wealthy families, often absentees, and worked by tenant farmers and day laborers who lived from one day's wage to the next. Withholding wages could mean hunger (5:4).
  • Famine. A severe famine struck Judea around AD 46–48 (Acts 11:28). Queen Helena of Adiabene bought grain from Egypt to relieve Jerusalem.
  • Courts. The rich could drag the poor into court (2:6), where status counted heavily.
  • The gold ring. In the Roman world a gold ring marked the wealthy equestrian class. A man “with a gold ring, in fine clothing” (2:2) was obviously important.
  • Unrest. In the 50s Judea saw bandits, assassins (sicarii) who stabbed opponents in crowds, and armed rebels. “Whence come wars and whence come fightings among you?” (4:1).
  • Merchants. Jewish traders traveled the empire's cities for business (4:13), a life full of risk.

Under Roman rule, the poor had little power, but James reminds them that God has chosen “them that are poor as to the world to be rich in faith” (2:5).

Jerusalem and the Dispersion

Far more Jews lived outside Judea than inside it; James writes from the mother church to believers among them.

  • The Dispersion. Large Jewish communities lived in Alexandria, Antioch, Rome, Asia Minor, Babylonia and beyond. Estimates run to several million Jews in the diaspora.
  • Synagogues. James uses the word “synagogue” for the believers' assembly (2:2), fitting Jewish Christians who still met in a synagogue-like setting.
  • The Jerusalem church. Under James it remained Jewish in practice and respected among many Jews; Josephus says James' execution outraged law-abiding people in the city.
  • Scattered by persecution. After Stephen's death believers were scattered as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch (Acts 11:19). Some of James' readers may have been among them.
  • Rains. The “early and latter rain” (5:7) are the autumn and spring rains of the land of Israel, on which every harvest depended.
  • Elijah. James' readers knew the story of Elijah's prayer stopping and starting the rain (5:17–18), a vivid image in a land where drought meant famine.

The time map

The shaded band marks the early dating. If written later, James belongs near the end of his life, as tensions in Judea were rising toward war.

How the setting shapes the study

James' sayings are drawn from everyday life.

PassageConnection to the times
Jas 1:6A wave of the sea driven by the wind: sea travel was common for diaspora Jews.
Jas 1:10–11Grass and flowers wither quickly under the hot east wind of the region.
Jas 2:2–3A gold ring marked high rank; seating in assemblies reflected status.
Jas 2:6The rich dragged the poor before courts.
Jas 3:3–4Bits in horses' mouths and rudders of ships: small things controlling large ones.
Jas 3:5–6A small fire could set a whole hillside of brush ablaze in the dry season.
Jas 4:13–14Traveling merchants planned business trips to other cities.
Jas 5:4Day laborers were paid at day's end; withheld wages meant hunger.
Jas 5:14Oil was a common medicine as well as a sign of God's blessing.

James writes like a prophet and a wise teacher, with Jesus' own sayings ringing behind his words.

items.text: Greeting
James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes which are of the Dispersion, greeting.
Testing of Your Faith
Count it all joy, my brethren, when ye fall into manifold temptations;
knowing that the proving of your faith worketh patience.
And let patience have its perfect work, that ye may be perfect and entire, lacking in nothing.
But if any of you lacketh wisdom, let him ask of God, who giveth to all liberally and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.
But let him ask in faith, nothing doubting: for he that doubteth is like the surge of the sea driven by the wind and tossed.
For let not that man think that he shall receive anything of the Lord;
a doubleminded man, unstable in all his ways.
But let the brother of low degree glory in his high estate:
and the rich, in that he is made low: because as the flower of the grass he shall pass away.
For the sun ariseth with the scorching wind, and withereth the grass; and the flower thereof falleth, and the grace of the fashion of it perisheth: so also shall the rich man fade away in his goings.
Blessed is the man that endureth temptation; for when he hath been approved, he shall receive the crown of life, which the Lord promised to them that love him.
Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God; for God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempteth no man:
but each man is tempted, when he is drawn away by his own lust, and enticed.
Then the lust, when it hath conceived, beareth sin: and the sin, when it is fullgrown, bringeth forth death.
Be not deceived, my beloved brethren.
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation, neither shadow that is cast by turning.
Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.
Hearing and Doing the Word
Ye know this, my beloved brethren. But let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:
for the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.
Wherefore putting away all filthiness and overflowing of wickedness, receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.
But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deluding your own selves.
For if any one is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a mirror:
for he beholdeth himself, and goeth away, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was.
But he that looketh into the perfect law, the law of liberty, and so continueth, being not a hearer that forgetteth but a doer that worketh, this man shall be blessed in his doing.
If any man thinketh himself to be religious, while he bridleth not his tongue but deceiveth his heart, this man’s religion is vain.
Pure religion and undefiled before our God and Father is this, to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unspotted from the world.

summary.title: CHAPTER 1 IN SUMMARY
paras: James greets the twelve tribes in the Dispersion and begins at once: “Count it all joy… when ye fall into manifold temptations,” because the testing of faith produces patience, which leads to maturity. Anyone who lacks wisdom should ask God in faith, without doubting. The poor believer should boast in his high position, and the rich in his humiliation, for wealth fades like a flower. Blessed is the one who endures trial.

God does not tempt anyone; temptation comes from one's own desire, which leads to sin and death. Every good gift comes from the Father of lights, who gave us new birth by the word of truth. So everyone should be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger, and receive the implanted word with meekness. “But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only,” for whoever hears without doing is like a man who forgets his face after looking in a mirror. Pure religion is to visit orphans and widows in their affliction and keep oneself unspotted from the world.

items.text: The Sin of Partiality
My brethren, hold not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons.
For if there come into your synagogue a man with a gold ring, in fine clothing, and there come in also a poor man in vile clothing;
and ye have regard to him that weareth the fine clothing, and say, Sit thou here in a good place; and ye say to the poor man, Stand thou there, or sit under my footstool;
do ye not make distinctions among yourselves, and become judges with evil thoughts?
Hearken, my beloved brethren; did not God choose them that are poor as to the world to be rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he promised to them that love him?
But ye have dishonored the poor man. Do not the rich oppress you, and themselves drag you before the judgment-seats?
Do not they blaspheme the honorable name by which ye are called?
Howbeit if ye fulfil the royal law, according to the scripture, Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself, ye do well:
but if ye have respect of persons, ye commit sin, being convicted by the law as transgressors.
For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet stumble in one point, he is become guilty of all.
For he that said, Do not commit adultery, said also, Do not kill. Now if thou dost not commit adultery, but killest, thou art become a transgressor of the law.
So speak ye, and so do, as men that are to be judged by a law of liberty.
For judgment is without mercy to him that hath showed no mercy: mercy glorieth against judgment.
Faith Without Works Is Dead
What doth it profit, my brethren, if a man say he hath faith, but have not works? can that faith save him?
If a brother or sister be naked and in lack of daily food,

items.text: and one of you say unto them, Go in peace, be ye warmed and filled; and yet ye give them not the things needful to the body; what doth it profit?
Even so faith, if it have not works, is dead in itself.
Yea, a man will say, Thou hast faith, and I have works: show me thy faith apart from thy works, and I by my works will show thee my faith.
Thou believest that God is one; thou doest well: the demons also believe, and shudder.
But wilt thou know, O vain man, that faith apart from works is barren?
Was not Abraham our father justified by works, in that he offered up Isaac his son upon the altar?
Thou seest that faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect;
and the scripture was fulfilled which saith, And Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned unto him for righteousness; and he was called the friend of God.
Ye see that by works a man is justified, and not only by faith.
And in like manner was not also Rahab the harlot justified by works, in that she received the messengers, and sent them out another way?
For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, even so faith apart from works is dead.

summary.title: CHAPTER 2 IN SUMMARY
paras: Believers must not show favoritism. If a rich man with a gold ring and fine clothing comes into their assembly and they give him a good seat, while telling a poor man to stand, they have become judges with evil thoughts. God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith, while it is the rich who oppress them. To show partiality is to break the royal law, “Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself,” and whoever stumbles in one point is guilty of all. Mercy triumphs over judgment.

What good is it if someone says he has faith but has no works? If a brother or sister lacks food and you only say, “Go in peace, be ye warmed and filled,” what good is that? “Even so faith, if it have not works, is dead in itself.” Even the demons believe that God is one, and tremble. Abraham's faith was completed by his works when he offered Isaac, and Rahab was justified when she received the messengers. “For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, even so faith apart from works is dead.”

items.text: Taming the Tongue
Be not many of you teachers, my brethren, knowing that we shall receive heavier judgment.
For in many things we all stumble. If any stumbleth not in word, the same is a perfect man, able to bridle the whole body also.
Now if we put the horses’ bridles into their mouths that they may obey us, we turn about their whole body also.
Behold, the ships also, though they are so great and are driven by rough winds, are yet turned about by a very small rudder, whither the impulse of the steersman willeth.
So the tongue also is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how much wood is kindled by how small a fire!
And the tongue is a fire: the world of iniquity among our members is the tongue, which defileth the whole body, and setteth on fire the wheel of nature, and is set on fire by hell.
For every kind of beasts and birds, of creeping things and things in the sea, is tamed, and hath been tamed by mankind:
but the tongue can no man tame; it is a restless evil, it is full of deadly poison.
Therewith bless we the Lord and Father; and therewith curse we men, who are made after the likeness of God:
out of the same mouth cometh forth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be.
Doth the fountain send forth from the same opening sweet water and bitter?
can a fig tree, my brethren, yield olives, or a vine figs? neither can salt water yield sweet.
Wisdom from Above
Who is wise and understanding among you? let him show by his good life his works in meekness of wisdom.
But if ye have bitter jealousy and faction in your heart, glory not and lie not against the truth.
This wisdom is not a wisdom that cometh down from above, but is earthly, sensual, devilish.
For where jealousy and faction are, there is confusion and every vile deed.
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, easy to be entreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without variance, without hypocrisy.
And the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace for them that make peace.

summary.title: CHAPTER 3 IN SUMMARY
paras: Not many should become teachers, for they will be judged more strictly. We all stumble in many ways, and whoever never stumbles in what he says is perfect. Like a bit in a horse's mouth or a small rudder on a great ship, the tongue is small but powerful; like a little fire that sets a great forest ablaze, it can set the whole course of life on fire. People can tame every kind of animal, but no one can tame the tongue. With it we bless God and curse people made in His likeness; this ought not to be.

Who is wise and understanding? Let him show it by good conduct in the meekness of wisdom. Bitter jealousy and selfish ambition are not wisdom from above but earthly, natural and demonic, producing disorder and every vile practice. “But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, easy to be entreated, full of mercy and good fruits.” The fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

items.text: Submit Yourselves to God
Whence come wars and whence come fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your pleasures that war in your members?
Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and covet, and cannot obtain: ye fight and war; ye have not, because ye ask not.
Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may spend it in your pleasures.
Ye adulteresses, know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God? Whosoever therefore would be a friend of the world maketh himself an enemy of God.
Or think ye that the scripture speaketh in vain? Doth the spirit which he made to dwell in us long unto envying?
But he giveth more grace. Wherefore the scripture saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace to the humble.
Be subject therefore unto God; but resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you. Cleanse your hands, ye sinners; and purify your hearts, ye doubleminded.
Be afflicted, and mourn, and weep: let your laughter be turned to mourning, and your joy to heaviness.
Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall exalt you.

Speak not one against another, brethren. He that speaketh against a brother, or judgeth his brother, speaketh against the law, and judgeth the law: but if thou judgest the law, thou art not a doer of the law, but a judge.
One only is the lawgiver and judge, even he who is able to save and to destroy: but who art thou that judgest thy neighbor?
Boasting About Tomorrow
Come now, ye that say, To-day or to-morrow we will go into this city, and spend a year there, and trade, and get gain:
whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. What is your life? For ye are a vapor that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.
For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall both live, and do this or that.
But now ye glory in your vauntings: all such glorying is evil.
To him therefore that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin.

summary.title: CHAPTER 4 IN SUMMARY
paras: Quarrels and fights come from passions at war within. People covet and do not have, so they fight; they do not have because they do not ask, or ask with wrong motives. Friendship with the world is enmity with God. But He gives more grace: “God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace to the humble.” So submit to God, resist the devil and he will flee, draw near to God and He will draw near to you, and humble yourselves before the Lord, and He will exalt you. Do not speak evil of one another, for only God is judge.

To those who say, “To-day or to-morrow we will go into this city, and spend a year there, and trade, and get gain,” James replies that they do not know what tomorrow will bring: “What is your life? For ye are a vapor.” They should say instead, “If the Lord will, we shall both live, and do this or that.” Boasting in arrogance is evil, and whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, sins.

items.text: Warning to the Rich
Come now, ye rich, weep and howl for your miseries that are coming upon you.
Your riches are corrupted, and your garments are moth-eaten.
Your gold and your silver are rusted; and their rust shall be for a testimony against you, and shall eat your flesh as fire. Ye have laid up your treasure in the last days.
Behold, the hire of the laborers who mowed your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth out: and the cries of them that reaped have entered into the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth.
Ye have lived delicately on the earth, and taken your pleasure; ye have nourished your hearts in a day of slaughter.
Ye have condemned, ye have killed the righteous one; he doth not resist you.
Patience in Suffering
Be patient therefore, brethren, until the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receive the early and latter rain.
Be ye also patient; establish your hearts: for the coming of the Lord is at hand.
Murmur not, brethren, one against another, that ye be not judged: behold, the judge standeth before the doors.
Take, brethren, for an example of suffering and of patience, the prophets who spake in the name of the Lord.
Behold, we call them blessed that endured: ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord, how that the Lord is full of pity, and merciful.
But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by the heaven, nor by the earth, nor by any other oath: but let your yea be yea, and your nay, nay; that ye fall not under judgment.
The Prayer of Faith
Is any among you suffering? let him pray. Is any cheerful? let him sing praise.
Is any among you sick? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord:
and the prayer of faith shall save him that is sick, and the Lord shall raise him up; and if he have committed sins, it shall be forgiven him.
Confess therefore your sins one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The supplication of a righteous man availeth much in its working.
Elijah was a man of like passions with us, and he prayed fervently that it might not rain; and it rained not on the earth for three years and six months.
And he prayed again; and the heaven gave rain, and the earth brought forth her fruit.
My brethren, if any among you err from the truth, and one convert him;
let him know, that he who converteth a sinner from the error of his way shall save a soul from death, and shall cover a multitude of sins.

summary.title: CHAPTER 5 IN SUMMARY
paras: James warns the rich oppressors to weep and howl for the miseries coming on them. Their riches have rotted and their gold is rusted, a witness against them. The wages of the laborers who mowed their fields, which they kept back by fraud, cry out, and the cries have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts. They have lived in luxury and condemned and killed the righteous. Believers should be patient until the coming of the Lord, as a farmer waits for the early and latter rain, and not grumble against one another, taking the prophets and Job as examples of endurance. Do not swear oaths; let your yes be yes. Is anyone suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone sick? Let him call the elders to pray over him and anoint him with oil, and the prayer of faith will save the sick. Confess sins to one another and pray for one another, for the prayer of a righteous man is powerful, as Elijah's was. Whoever brings back a wanderer from the truth will save a soul from death.

wrap.title: James In Summary
paras: James is a letter about faith that works. Writing to Jewish believers scattered across the Roman world, many of them poor and under pressure, James gives a series of direct, practical commands about how a real follower of Jesus lives. His style is like the Old Testament wisdom books and the prophets, and it echoes Jesus' Sermon on the Mount again and again.

James begins with trials. Hard times test faith and produce endurance and maturity, so believers can count them joy and ask God for wisdom. Temptation never comes from God, who gives only good gifts. The key is to receive God's word humbly and then do it: “be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only.”

James is especially concerned about the poor. Favoring the rich in church gatherings breaks the royal law of love. Faith that sees a hungry brother and does nothing is dead. The rich landowners who withhold their workers' wages will face God's judgment, and the poor should wait patiently for the Lord's coming, like a farmer waiting for rain.

James' teaching on faith and works is sometimes thought to contradict Paul, but they address different problems. Paul insists that we are made right with God by faith, not by works of the Law; James insists that genuine faith always shows itself in works. Both agree that a faith that does not change one's life is not saving faith.

James also deals with the tongue, worldly ambition, arrogant planning, oaths, sickness and prayer. The message in one line: true faith in Jesus is not just words but a changed life, shown in endurance, care for the poor, controlled speech, humility before God and persistent prayer.
